segments.title: Why the planned names signalled national purpose
segments.summary: The planned Lexington-class names show that the US Navy expected the battlecruisers to carry unusual political and national weight.
segments.body: The six projected ships were Lexington, Constellation, Saratoga, Ranger, Constitution, and United States. Battleships already drew their names from states, and the Navy could have extended the Revolutionary War pattern of Lexington and Saratoga with names such as Concord. Constitution, United States, and Constellation carried greater national prestige. A ship named United States entering a foreign port would advertise American interest with unusual directness. The names suited ships intended to advertise American power abroad as well as fight.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the planned names, contrasts them with state and battle names, and links the most prestigious choices to American interests.

segments.title: Moving the Constitution name to a battlecruiser
segments.summary: The official renaming of the historic USS Constitution shows how seriously the Navy prepared to transfer the name to CC-1.
segments.body: CC-1, ordered from Fore River at Quincy, was initially meant to be Constitution; the hull later took the name Lexington and became an aircraft carrier. To free the name, the historic frigate USS Constitution was officially renamed Old Constitution from 1 December 1917 until 24 July 1925. If CC-1 had entered service first as Constitution, the ships might have been remembered as the Constitution class. The paperwork and long renaming period show that this was a firm naval plan. That exceptional name suited a ship intended for peacetime presence and wartime scouting.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies CC-1's planned Constitution name, the frigate's temporary Old Constitution name, and the class's combined presence and wartime scouting purposes.

segments.title: Battlecruisers as peacetime presence ships
segments.summary: A fast, imposing Lexington could have projected US naval power through world cruises and diplomatic visits before combat.
segments.body: Even before construction, polished renderings made the Lexingtons part of peacetime information warfare. The clipper bow, low quarterdeck, large guns, twin funnels, and tall masts advertised speed and force. Completed ships could have taken the same sort of world tour as Hood and Repulse on the Royal Navy's Empire Cruise, visiting Japan, China, India, Australia, Europe, Britain, and South America. Each port call would have linked American diplomacy to a memorable capital ship. Later encounters with smaller US cruisers, sloops, or gunboats could revive that image, extending the battlecruisers' influence beyond their immediate presence.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the design's visual impact, planned world travel, diplomatic visits, and the lasting impression that reinforced smaller US Navy ships.

segments.title: Scouting, information denial, and Japanese rivals
segments.summary: The class was meant to secure American scouting and contest Japanese battlecruisers such as the Kongōs and planned Amagis.
segments.body: Wartime information warfare meant keeping the American scouting force alive and able to report. Kongō-class battlecruisers could threaten US cruisers gathering intelligence, while the planned Amagi class raised the danger further. The proposed American battlecruisers would cover reconnaissance and challenge the ships sent to disrupt it. The framework separates those tasks into information acquisition and information denial. Combining them made combat against enemy capital ships part of the Lexington requirement.

evidence.note: The transcript connects the wartime scouting role to the Kongō and planned Amagi threats, then distinguishes information acquisition from information denial.

segments.title: From presence ship to fast battleship
segments.summary: A spectrum from presence and scouting work to sustained capital-ship combat explains why later battlecruisers needed more protection.
segments.body: The distinction between 'battle cruiser' and 'battlecruiser' describes changing design priorities. Invincible and Indefatigable sit near the presence, commerce, and scouting end of the spectrum. Lion and Queen Mary move toward a heavier fighting role, while Tiger and especially Hood approach the fast-battleship end. Ships expected to trade sustained capital-ship fire need protection that lets them absorb punishment while returning it. Lexington's design therefore has to be judged by its intended employment, rather than by armour figures alone.

evidence.note: The transcript places Invincible, Indefatigable, Lion, Queen Mary, Tiger, Hood, fast battleships, and battleships on a spectrum of capital-ship roles.

segments.title: The speed and protection trade-off
segments.summary: Lexington suited presence, commerce, and scouting work, while direct capital-ship combat exposed the cost of her limited protection.
segments.body: Lexington suited peacetime presence, economic warfare, and scouting, where speed and offensive power carried much of the burden. Direct combat with enemy capital ships exposed the cost of her lighter protection. The stated scheme included a five-to-seven-inch belt, five-to-nine-inch barbettes, eleven-inch turret faces, six-inch turret sides, a twelve-inch conning tower, and a deck between one and a half and two and a quarter inches. Hood provides the immediate comparison: her belt reached twelve inches, turret armour ranged from eleven to fifteen inches, and barbettes from five to twelve inches, although some deck areas were thinner than Lexington's. The comparison shows why a design suited to presence and reconnaissance became vulnerable once it was expected to fight enemy capital ships.

evidence.note: The transcript evaluates Lexington against its intended role, gives its armour figures, and begins the armour comparison with Hood.

segments.title: Comparing Lexington with HMS Hood
segments.summary: The comparison sets Lexington's speed, range, 16-inch battery, and turbo-electric machinery against Hood's heavier protection.
segments.body: Lexington and Hood were contemporaries that divided weight and machinery differently. Lexington was credited with 33 knots and 10,000 nautical miles at 10 knots; Hood with 32 knots and 5,332 nautical miles at 20 knots. Lexington carried four twin 16-inch mountings, while Hood had four twin 15-inch mountings. Sixteen water-tube boilers fed Lexington's turbo-electric drive for 180,000 shaft horsepower across four shafts; Hood's twenty-four Yarrow boilers and geared turbines produced 144,000 shaft horsepower. The extra 36,000 horsepower bought Lexington one knot. Lexington is quoted at about 44,200 tons near standard load and 45,304 tons deep, compared with Hood's 47,430 tons deep. These figures show how the shared battlecruiser label concealed different choices about propulsion and protection.

evidence.note: The transcript compares range, speed, main batteries, boilers, propulsion systems, horsepower, and displacement for Lexington and Hood.

segments.title: A six-ship programme across American yards
segments.summary: Six hulls divided among four American yards show the industrial reach of the programme.
segments.body: The passage works through the hull numbers, planned names, dates, and builders for all six ships. The first four hulls went to Fore River, Newport News, and New York Shipbuilding, with Newport News receiving two. Philadelphia Naval Shipyard received CC-5 Constitution and CC-6 United States, both laid down on 25 September 1920, the same date given for Saratoga. With two hulls each at Newport News and Philadelphia, the six-ship programme engaged four yards. The distribution shows how much American shipbuilding capacity the Navy had committed before the treaty ended the class.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the six hulls, changing names, laying-down dates, and their distribution among four shipyards.

segments.title: Why the portholes in a later rendering may mislead
segments.summary: Some apparent portholes in a later Lexington rendering may have been deleted or painted rather than openings through the armour belt.
segments.body: A later rendering shows the design after further development and depicts many apparent portholes along the hull. Some openings may have disappeared from the final plan. Others may have been painted shapes intended to look like portholes from a distance while the belt remained solid. Artwork for an unbuilt warship therefore requires caution when used as evidence for the final construction plan.

evidence.note: The transcript returns to a later design image, identifies its many apparent portholes, and cautions that some may have been removed or painted rather than true openings through the belt.

segments.title: Pacific employment and fleet-support assumptions
segments.summary: The design makes more sense as a Pacific fleet asset expected to avoid unsupported duels with stronger enemy battlecruisers.
segments.body: The design began as a presence and economic-warfare ship, which may have shaped assumptions about its use across the Pacific. The operating concept may have kept Lexingtons from meeting enemy battlecruisers alone or in unsupported pairs. They might fight Kongō-class ships directly, while the more formidable Amagis presented a harder problem. One possible tactic was to draw those opponents toward Colorado-class or later US battleships. Fleet cooperation could therefore turn Lexington's speed and scouting ability into practical strengths despite limited protection.

evidence.note: The transcript considers Pacific employment, distinguishes Kongō and Amagi as opponents, and proposes drawing enemy battlecruisers toward Colorado-class or later US battleships.

segments.title: Why treaty survival would encourage heavy modernization
segments.summary: Treaty limits would have made surviving Lexingtons scarce, fast capital ships and strong candidates for repeated modernization.
segments.body: A counterfactual fleet completes Admiral-class ships, G3s, and Lexingtons in different combinations, including a possible three-and-three split between battlecruisers and aircraft carriers. If a later treaty stopped new capital-ship construction, the surviving Lexingtons would rank among the fastest and most adaptable large hulls available. Their weaknesses would create an immediate list of upgrades, while their unusual speed would make replacement or disposal unattractive. Repeated reconstruction would follow from scarcity as much as from flaws in the original design. Arms-control limits could therefore prolong the service and transformation of imperfect ships.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes mixed battlecruiser and carrier completions, then argues that treaty-limited survivors would receive extensive modernization.

segments.title: The capital ships that might have followed Lexington
segments.summary: Without an arms-control halt, completed Lexington, G3, N3, Colorado, South Dakota, Nagato, Amagi, and Francesco Caracciolo programmes would have forced another round of capital-ship design.
segments.body: With treaty limits removed, the question becomes what follows these programmes. The Royal Navy might field G3 battlecruisers and N3 battleships with 18-inch guns while the US Navy operates Colorados, Lexingtons, and possibly the 1920 South Dakotas. Japan adds Nagatos and Amagis, while Italy's Francesco Caracciolo class and possible French completions widen the competition. Designers would have to decide whether the successors still belonged among battlecruisers or had crossed into fast-battleship territory. Lexington becomes a starting point for an interwar capital-ship race that the treaty system prevented.

evidence.note: The transcript asks what follows Lexington, G3, and Amagi, then lists major British, American, Japanese, Italian, and French capital-ship possibilities.

segments.title: What treaty limits removed from naval planning
segments.summary: The cancelled programmes show which capabilities and industrial commitments governments accepted losing through naval arms control.
segments.body: Comparing the ships nations could have completed with the programmes they surrendered under treaty limits reveals their strategic priorities. The loss included individual hulls and the design paths that might have followed them. The long effort to reserve Constitution for CC-1 shows that the US Navy understood the status it expected from the class. The name ties treaty choices to the political, industrial, and diplomatic purposes introduced at the start of the episode.

evidence.note: The transcript explains how foregone ships and capabilities illuminate national priorities and returns to the Constitution name as evidence that the US Navy knew what it lost.
